list.listitem: In suspected cases of vestibular neuritis the immediate history and physical should focus on identifying risk factors or physical findings for stroke or other acute intracranial lesions. C

Patients with advanced age, significant risk factors for CVA, severe headache, inability to stand, vertical nystagmus, or other focal neurologic deficits should undergo imaging with an MRI of the head with contrast or CT scan with cerebellum views. C
Corticosteroids did not improve clinical recovery in one randomized clinical trial. B

If available, vestibular rehabilitation programs are effective for patients with unilateral peripheral vestibular dysfunction. A

background.definition: Vestibular neuritis is a clinical syndrome characterized by the abrupt onset of vertigo, lasting days to weeks. For the first few days symptoms are typically severe with nausea, vomiting, and balance disturbance. Hearing loss and tinnitus are usually absent. If hearing is affected it is called acute labyrinthitis.

list.listitem: All age groups, but peak ages are 30 years to 50 years.
Both sexes affected equally.
The incidence is said to be 3.5/100,000 per year, but this figure is likely an underestimate of true incidence.
Accounts for about 7% of patients at outpatient clinics specializing in vertigo treatment.
Up to one third of adults will experience prolonged anxiety after an episode of vestibular neuritis.
Residual, low-grade imbalance may persist for months.
Most likely viral; possibly a reactivation of a latent herpes simplex virus type 1 infection.
In approximately half of cases a preceding upper respiratory infection is reported.
In some cases vestibular neuritis may result from an autoimmune disorder.
Inflammation of the vestibular branch of the eighth cranial nerve.
May be direct viral infection or postviral immune modulated.
None
Suspect vestibular neuritis with acute onset of vertigo, nausea, and gait disturbance. C
Diagnosis is supported with a positive head thrust test. C
Further testing indicated in patients with advanced age, significant CVA risk factors, sudden onset of severe headache, inability to stand, vertical nystagmus, or other focal neurologic deficits. C
Imaging with an MRI of the head with contrast is preferred, but a CT scan with cerebellum views is appropriate when MRI is contraindicated or unavailable. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Acute vascular lesions of the CNS
Differential.Differential_Features: Central nystagmus, inability to stand, other neurologic deficits, new or severe headache
Brief (usually less than a minute) episodic vertigo associated with head movement
Recurrent vertigo associated with hearing loss and tinnitus

list.listitem: Rapid onset (within hours) of vertigo, nausea, and imbalance or gait disturbance with a sensation of falling to one side (toward the affected side).
A history of preceding viral illness is present in half of cases.

Positive head thrust test (patient asked to maintain focus straight ahead (or on examiner's nose) while examiner rapidly moves the head 5-10 degrees in a side-to-side rotation) with horizontal or horizontal-rotational component nystagmus, with the fast phase away from the affected side.
The patient may fall toward affected side with Romberg testing.

It is important to identify, if present, findings suggesting stroke or other intracranial lesion, including advanced age with significant risk factors for CVA, sudden onset of new or severe headache, inability to stand unsupported, vertical nystagmus, and any focal neurologic deficits.
Diagnosis is clinical, based on typical symptoms and an otherwise negative neurology exam.

Specialists use a variety of diagnostic maneuvers including otolith function tests (ocular torsion, subjective visual vertical, and vestibular evoked myogenic potential) and canal function tests (head-shaking nystagmus (HSN), caloric stimulation, and head-thrust testing). In a case series of 51 consecutive patients with unilateral vestibular neuritis, all patients had abnormal HSN, caloric, and head-thrust test results, and at least one otolith-related test abnormality; otolith test results returned to normal more quickly than canal function tests.
MRI is the imaging study of first choice. A CT scan with cerebellum views is a reasonable alternative.
Order MRI with contrast if stroke, hemorrhage, or other intracranial lesion is suspected.
Since the diagnosis is based on the clinical exam and history, testing is usually not necessary.

Imaging should be considered in older patients at an increased risk of CVA, patients with other neurologic symptoms (see differential diagnosis), the onset of new or severe headache, and those who do not improve in 48 hours.
See algorithm in .

Corticosteroids did not improve clinical recovery in the single best trial measuring this outcome but did reduce vestibular paresis as measured by caloric testing at 12 months in another study. Overall there is insufficient evidence of symptomatic improvement. B
Symptomatic treatment includes antihistamines, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, or antiemetics. C
When possible, discontinue symptomatic treatment after 2 to 3 days to avoid suppressing the central compensation response. C
Vestibular exercises and rehabilitation programs are effective for patients with unilateral peripheral vestibular dysfunction. A

In a metaanalysis of 4 trials of corticosteroids vs. placebo, studies were small and of poor quality. There was some benefit in terms of complete caloric recovery at one month (RR 2.81), there was no effect on complete caloric recovery at 12 months or on symptomatic recovery of vestibular function at any point.

Another trial comparing corticosteroids to vestibular exercises in 40 patients with acute vestibular neuritis reported greater disease resolution in the corticosteroids group at 6 months of follow-up, but similar outcomes at 12 months.
In one trial showing 12-month benefit on caloric recovery, methylprednisolone was started at 100 mg per day and tapered to 10 mg over 3 weeks.
Antiviral therapy has not been found to be effective.
Other symptomatic treatment includes antihistamines, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, or antiemetics. A nonoral route is often necessary.
Consider limiting symptomatic treatment to 48 hours. Longer therapy may suppress the central compensation response and delay long-term recovery.
Vestibular exercises and rehabilitation programs effective for patients with unilateral peripheral vestibular dysfunction.
Most patients fully recover after several weeks. C
Some patients may have persistent but less severe vertigo for months. C
Prolonged generalized anxiety occurs in up to one third of patients. C

In one long term (mean 4.9 years) follow-up study (N = 51), recurrent vestibular neuritis occurred in 1 patient but subsequent BPPV occurred in 5 patients; BPPV affected the posterior canal of the same ear and occurred predominantly in patients who had not fully recovered from vestibular neuritis. C
Elderly patients with vertigo symptoms have a significantly higher probability of CVA or intracranial hemorrhage as underlying cause.
Vertigo in children is most commonly associated with otitis media, ear surgery, and migraine headaches.
Steroid therapy has not been studied specifically in children.

algorithm.title: Algorithm for the Management of Suspected Vestibular Neuritis.

cell.label: Suspected VN: Patient with acute onset of vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and imbalance or gait disturbance.
Assess for risk factors for CVD, severe headache, or inability to stand. Perform head thrust test, Romberg, and thorough neurology exam.
Head thrust positive for peripheral nystagmus, Romberg positive toward affected side, and no focal neurologic deficits or significant risk factors for stroke?
Start methylprednisolone at 100 mg a day and taper. Treat acute symptoms with antihistamines, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, or antiemetics.
If any risk factors or other neurologic signs proceed with MRI of head with contrast.
